1345.title: Peh
1345.howItsDone: Jews open the Amidah, the central standing prayer, with the verse from Psalm 51 asking God to open their lips; Jewish law on speech, lashon hara, guards against harmful talk about others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ayin, the eye, and Hagar by the spring. Your line: ayin is an eye. Today, the letter right after the eye: the mouth.

Moses stands at the burning bush with one more objection, and this one is about his mouth. He tells God he has never been a man of words; he is slow of speech and slow of tongue. A toast, a phone call, a hard conversation: the excuse has a familiar shape. God answers with a question, who made a person's mouth, and then a promise: I will be with your mouth, and teach you what to say. The man whose words fill so much of the Torah starts out afraid to open his.
screen: `MOSES: I AM SLOW OF SPEECH.` → `WHO MADE A PERSON'S MOUTH?` → `I WILL BE WITH YOUR MOUTH.`

segments.voice: Peh means a mouth, and the letter makes a p or an f, the sounds your lips make. Four ways to open it. First, the shape. A printed peh can look like a mouth, curved open, with a small mark tucked inside. Some teachers say it's a tongue, waiting. Others say it's a reminder that a mouth holds something back as well as letting it out. Second, Moses. He thinks his mouth disqualifies him. God doesn't argue that he speaks well. God says the mouth was made, and help will come into it. Third, prayer. The Amidah, the standing prayer, is opened with a short line from the Psalms. In the King James words: "O Lord, open thou my lips; and my mouth shall shew forth thy praise." The Talmud discusses saying it there. Before the prayer's own words begin, a person asks for help just to open their mouth. Fourth, the guard. Another psalm asks God to set a watch before the mouth and keep the door of the lips. Jewish ethics has a whole body of law about speech, lashon hara, the evil tongue, warning against harmful talk about others even when it's true. So the mouth here is a door. It opens for praise, teaching and comfort, and it has a doorkeeper. The same peh that can bless can wound, and the tradition takes both seriously. Moses's slow mouth ended up carrying words people still read aloud.

segments.voice: Close your mouth gently and breathe through your nose for a few breaths, noticing how rarely your mouth rests. Then bring to mind one person who would be glad to hear something kind from you, and find the words: true, small and specific, not you're great, but the way you handled that meeting was brave. If you pray, you can ask for help opening your lips.

1346.title: Tzadi
1346.hook: the letter of tzaddik, the righteous one
1346.howItsDone: Jews learn tzadi as the letter of tzaddik, the righteous person, and of tzedakah, the giving to people in need that Jewish law treats as an obligation rather than a choice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, peh, the mouth, and Moses slow of speech. Your line: peh is a mouth. Today, a letter with a whole person in its name.

One short phrase in one verse has kept readers arguing. It's about Noah. In the King James words: "Noah was a just man and perfect in his generations." Just translates the Hebrew tzaddik, righteous. Fine. But why add in his generations? Is the Torah praising him for staying good in a violent age? Or quietly holding back, saying he only looked good next to the people around him? The rabbis heard it both ways, and kept both. Today's letter begins the word they were arguing about.
screen: `NOAH: A JUST MAN.` → `IN HIS GENERATIONS.` → `PRAISE, OR A HEDGE?`

segments.voice: Tzadi makes a ts sound, and it begins tzaddik, a righteous person. Four angles. First, the argument. In the Talmud, one sage says: in his generations, and all the more so had he lived among good people, he would have been greater. Another says: in his generations, but not in others. Rashi puts the second view sharply: next to Abraham, he would have counted for little. Rashi brings both readings side by side and doesn't pick. Second, the word itself. A tzaddik in the Torah is not a statue. Noah is called righteous, and a few chapters later he plants a vineyard and gets drunk. The title doesn't mean flawless. It means a life that leans toward what's right, in a real time and place. Third, the family. Tzaddik shares its root with tzedek, justice, and tzedakah, the giving Jews owe to people in need. In Jewish law tzedakah isn't optional generosity; it's what righteousness looks like with money in its hand. Fourth, the foundation. Proverbs says, in the King James words, "the righteous is an everlasting foundation." Jewish teachers read it as a picture of the tzaddik: someone the world quietly rests on. Not loud, not perfect. Load bearing. So righteousness here isn't a feeling or a reputation. It's measured in acts, done in your own generation, among the people you actually live with, whether or not anyone better is watching.

Where is something a little unjust, or a little undone, like a bill a friend can't cover, a coworker taking blame that isn't theirs, a donation you meant to make? Choose one act you could actually do, not a feeling about it, and picture it start to finish. If you pray, you can ask for the nerve.

1347.title: Kuf
1347.howItsDone: Jews say the words of Isaiah 6:3 in the Kedushah during the repetition of the Amidah, and make kiddush over wine to set Shabbat apart; Leviticus 19, which opens with "be holy", is read in the yearly Torah cycle.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tzadi, and Noah, righteous in his generations. Your line: tzadi for tzaddik. Today, the letter that begins holy.

"Ye shall be holy: for I the LORD your God am holy." That's how Leviticus nineteen begins, in the King James words. It sounds like the start of something about temples and altars. There's an offering or two, but mostly something else. The same chapter tells you to leave the corners of your field for the poor, to pay a worker before the night is out, not to curse the deaf or trip the blind, to love your neighbor as yourself. Holiness, here, shows up at the edge of a field and on payday.
screen: `YE SHALL BE HOLY.` → `THE CORNERS OF THE FIELD.` → `PAY THE WORKER TONIGHT.`

segments.voice: Kuf makes a k sound, deep in the back of the mouth, and it begins kadosh, holy. Four steps. First, the root. Kadosh carries the sense of set apart, marked off for something. Holy things in Hebrew aren't necessarily shiny. They are distinct, given a different use. Second, a day. Early in Genesis, God rests on the seventh day, and in the King James words, "God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it." Sanctified is the same root. Before the story has a sanctuary or a priest, it has a holy day. Jews meet that root on Friday night in kiddush, the blessing over wine that sets Shabbat apart. Third, a cry. Isaiah sees angels calling to one another, "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory." Jews say those words in the Kedushah, a part of the service whose name means holiness, some rising on their toes as they say them. Fourth, the hands. Leviticus nineteen, which opens with be holy, fills itself with ordinary acts: fair weights, honest wages, respect for the old. Kiddush, Kaddish, Kedushah, kadosh: one letter and root run through wine, mourning, prayer and law. Holiness isn't kept on a mountain. It's set apart inside a field, a market, a workday. In this reading, something becomes holy when it's given a purpose beyond itself and treated that way.

segments.voice: Think back over the last day and look for one moment that felt set apart, even slightly: the first sip of coffee in a quiet kitchen, a child's hand in yours, a fair deal honestly made, a stranger who held a door. It doesn't need to be religious to count. Hold it for a few breaths and ask what made it different from the minutes around it; if you pray, you can give thanks for it.

1348.title: Resh
1348.hook: rosh, head, as in Rosh Hashanah
1348.howItsDone: Jews celebrate Rosh Hashanah, the head of the year, on the first day of the seventh month, with the blowing of the shofar; the Mishnah in tractate Rosh Hashanah counts four new years for different purposes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kuf, and holiness at the edge of a field. Your line: kuf for kadosh. Today, the letter of the head.

When does the Jewish year begin? Still in Egypt, before the Exodus, God tells Moses and Aaron about a month in spring. In the King James words: "This month shall be unto you the beginning of months: it shall be the first month of the year to you." Yet the Jewish New Year, Rosh Hashanah, falls in autumn, in the seventh month. In the Torah, that day is simply the first day of the seventh month, a day of blowing the horn. So, spring or fall? The answer turns on one small word.
screen: `SPRING: THE BEGINNING OF MONTHS.` → `ROSH HASHANAH IN THE SEVENTH MONTH.` → `WHERE DOES THE YEAR BEGIN?`

segments.voice: Resh makes an r sound, and it begins rosh, head. Rosh Hashanah is literally the head of the year. Four parts. First, the heads of the year. The Mishnah, in the tractate named for this holiday, answers our puzzle: there are four new years. One in spring, for counting the reign of kings and the order of the festivals. One in late summer, for tithing animals. One in autumn, for counting years. One in winter, for trees. A year can have more than one head, depending on what you're counting. Second, the beginning. From rosh comes reshit, beginning. The Torah's first word, bereshit, in the beginning, carries it. So does a line in Psalms, in the King James words: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom." Third, the shape. Resh looks a lot like dalet, the door; the difference is one corner, sharp on dalet, rounded on resh. In the Shema, the last letter of echad, one, is a dalet, and scribes write it large. Some commentators say it's so no one mistakes it for a resh, which would turn one into acher, another. Fourth, the head itself. Rosh is the part of you that goes first, that sees before the hands move. Rosh Hashanah isn't only a new number on the calendar; it's a day for taking stock before the year runs. A head, in this tradition, is a place to start from, and a place to think from.

If you pray, you can ask for a clear head.

1349.title: Shin
1349.hook: the letter on the mezuzah, standing for Shaddai
1349.howItsDone: Jewish homes fix a mezuzah, a case holding a handwritten parchment of the Shema passages, on the right-hand doorpost, often marked with the letter shin for Shaddai; some Jews touch it and kiss their fingers as they pass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, resh, the head of the year. Your line: resh for rosh. Today, a letter you can find on a doorframe.

A hallway of apartment doors, and on some, a small case fixed to the right-hand doorpost, often set at a slant. Wood, metal, glass, clay, sometimes a child's art project. Often there's one letter on it, raised or painted: three upright strokes joined at the bottom, like a crown, or a little flame with three tongues. People pass it every day on the way to work and the grocery store. Some reach up and touch it as they go. Today's letter is that one.
screen: `A SMALL CASE ON THE DOORPOST.` → `THREE STROKES, JOINED AT THE BASE.` → `TOUCHED ON THE WAY OUT.`

segments.voice: Shin makes a sh sound, three arms rising from one base. The case is a mezuzah, and mezuzah means doorpost. Four steps toward the door. First, the command. Inside the case is a small parchment, written by hand, with passages from Deuteronomy, including the Shema, whose first word begins with shin. One line gives the case its job. In the King James words: "And thou shalt write them upon the posts of thy house, and on thy gates." Second, the name. The shin on the outside is usually explained as standing for Shaddai, a name of God. When God appears to Abram in Genesis, the King James words are "I am the Almighty God," in Hebrew, El Shaddai. On many mezuzah parchments, Shaddai is also written on the back, facing out. Third, a later reading. Some teachers read the letters of Shaddai as initials for a phrase meaning guardian of the doors of Israel. That's a reading added later, not the plain meaning of the name, but it shows what people hoped a door could hold. Fourth, the touch. Some Jews touch the mezuzah going in or out, and some kiss their fingers after. It takes less than a second, and it turns one of the plainest places in a home into a moment of remembering, right where you cross from private to public and back. The Shema says to keep these words in your heart, then puts them on the door, where your body passes them whether your heart is ready or not.

1350.title: Tav (Shabbat 104a)
1350.hook: emet, truth, uses the first, middle and last letters: truth spans everything
1350.howItsDone: Jewish learners study the letters of emet and sheker through the Talmud's teaching in Shabbat 104a; the word emet is also said in daily prayer right after the Shema.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shin, the letter on the doorpost. Your line: shin on the door. Today, the last letter of the alef-bet.

Write the Hebrew word for a lie: sheker. Three letters, shin, kuf, resh. In the alef-bet they sit right next to each other near the end, crowded together. Now write the word for truth: emet. Alef, mem, tav. Alef stands at the very start, tav at the very end, mem between them. To spell the truth, you have to reach across the whole thing. The rabbis noticed this, and they didn't think it was an accident. Today, the letter that finishes the word, and the alef-bet.
screen: `SHEKER: THREE NEIGHBORS.` → `EMET: ALEF, MEM, TAV.` → `ACROSS THE WHOLE ALEF-BET.`

segments.voice: Tav makes a t sound, it's the last of the letters, and in tractate Shabbat the rabbis read the end of the alef-bet like a parable. Four readings. First, the span. Emet starts with the first letter, passes through the middle, and ends with the last. Truth, the reading goes, has to be true at the beginning, the middle and the end. A story honest only at the start isn't emet. Second, the crowd. The letters of sheker huddle together in one corner. The Talmud asks why, and answers: falsehood is easy to come by, and truth is hard to find. Lies are close at hand; truth takes a reach. Third, the feet. The letters of sheker, the rabbis say, each stand on a single leg. The letters of emet stand on broad bases, like bricks. Put simply: truth stands, and falsehood does not stand. A lie needs propping up; truth can bear weight. Fourth, the seal. Elsewhere in the same tractate, the Talmud says the seal of the Holy One is emet, truth. A seal is the mark at the end of a letter that says who it's from, and tav, the last letter, is where the seal goes. So the run of letters that began with a silent alef closes here, and the rabbis put truth across the whole span between them.
screen: `EMET: FIRST, MIDDLE, LAST.` · `SHEKER: NEIGHBORS IN A CORNER.` · `TRUTH STANDS; FALSEHOOD DOES NOT.` · `THE SEAL OF THE HOLY ONE IS TRUTH.` · then, large: `TRUTH FROM ALEF TO TAV.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small place where you've been leaning on a lie: not a scandal, an I'm fine that isn't, a yes you didn't mean, a story you've been telling yourself. Notice how much effort it takes to keep it standing on one leg, then find the true sentence that could stand on its own feet and say it silently to yourself. If you pray, you can ask for courage.

Your line: truth from alef to tav. Truth reaches the whole way. That's the whole alef-bet.

1351.title: Final letters
1351.hook: five letters change shape at the end of a word
1351.howItsDone: Hebrew writes five letters, kaf, mem, nun, peh and tzadi, in a final form (sofit) at the end of a word; the Talmud groups them under the made-up word mantzepach and discusses them in Shabbat 104a.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tav, the last letter, and emet spanning the whole alef-bet. Your line: truth from alef to tav. Today, the letters that change at the end.

Melech. King. Three letters: mem, lamed, kaf. At the start of a word, kaf is a rounded shape that sits on the line, like the cupped palm from a few days back. At the end of melech it straightens, and its tail drops below the line, as if the word were stepping off a curb. Same letter, same sound, new shape. And kaf isn't alone. Mem, which you met in mayim, does it too, and so do nun, peh and tzadi. The Talmud groups the five under one made-up word, mantzepach, built from the letters themselves.
screen: `MELECH: A KAF AT THE END.` → `SAME SOUND, NEW SHAPE.` → `MANTZEPACH: THE FIVE.`

segments.voice: Sofit means final, from sof, end. A mem sofit is a final mem. Four things to know. First, the shapes. Final mem closes into a box. Final kaf, nun, peh and tzadi drop a long tail below the line, as if leaning into the space after the word. Second, the seers. The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, says the final forms were spoken by the tzofim, the watchmen or seers. Then it raises a puzzle: if the Torah was given with them, how could later people have introduced them? Its answer: they were known, then forgotten, then restored. The rabbis cared enough about the shape of an ending to argue where it came from. Third, the bent and the straight. On the same page, the Talmud reads nun and tzadi as pairs. A bent nun and a straight nun: a person faithful when bent low will be faithful standing straight. A bent tzadi and a straight tzadi: the same for the righteous. Remember the nun that fell in Ashrei, and the tzadi of Noah in his generations. Here they get a second shape, upright at the end. Fourth, the week. It began with peh, the mouth, and Moses slow of speech. Then tzadi, the righteous one; kuf, holy; resh, the head of the year; shin on the doorpost; tav, the seal of truth; and now the endings. Two of this week's letters, peh and tzadi, have a final form of their own. In Hebrew, how a word ends shows on the page.
screen: `SOFIT: FINAL, FROM SOF, END.` · `A CLOSED BOX AND FOUR LONG TAILS.` · `THE SEERS SPOKE THEM, THE TALMUD SAYS.` · `BENT NOW, STRAIGHT AT THE END.` · then, large: `FIVE ENDINGS.`

segments.voice: With a pen, or a fingertip on your palm, draw a final nun: one straight stroke from the top down, past where the line would be, slowly, all the way. Then think of one thing ending in your life this week, a project, a season, a habit, a hard stretch, and ask whether you'd like it to end closed and complete like a final mem, or upright and reaching on like that nun. If you pray, you can bring it in.
Sofit. Final: the end form of five letters, kaf, mem, nun, peh and tzadi. Today's word.
Your line: five endings. An ending can stand up straight. A week of letters, done.
